p: Devin's cleanup shipped a bug. A Copilot suggestion had swapped a calendar helper for plain day math, so discharge windows that crossed the November clock change ended a day early.
Fourteen hospital tickets came in before Priya rolled it back.
Renata had approved it after reading three files, because Devin was senior and it was Friday. Priya told her she'd seen the times on Friday too, and gone home.
The incident writeup had no names in it, and a line from each of them owning their part.
Renata asked about the hour that happens twice. Devin brushed her off, she asked again, and he added the test.
On Halloween night Raj set every clock in the house back by hand.
Joyce Cho. The CTO. The board meets on the twelfth, and she wants something to show it.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. His rules live in his head.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. He's reading his own pull requests now.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer. She writes everything down.
Tomasz Nowak. Leads Kraków. His team took the date bug personally.
Ken Ito. Security lead. His scanner reads every pull request.

The clocks had gone back on Sunday and her body hadn't, so on Monday she was up an hour before she needed to be. Priya spent it at the kitchen table with her old runbook, the one with "ask Anders" written in the margins in her own handwriting, and counted. Twenty three.

Then she started a second list: the rules at Halcyon that weren't written down anywhere. A discharge window is calendar days, in the hospital's own time zone. Never build SQL by gluing strings together. Log request IDs, never request bodies. Run date tests in a time zone that changes its clocks. She stopped at eleven. Every one of them lived in somebody's head, and one had lived in the name of a helper function until a cleanup called it unused and deleted it.
At 6:50 a message came in from Tomasz in Kraków. Eight hours again. Our week as neighbors is over.

An email from Joyce Cho. Subject: The 12th. Elena's board is a week from Thursday. She'll ask one question about Copilot: what did we change so last week can't happen again. I'd like the answer to be something we can open and read. Joyce
Asha's cards came at 7:30, five photos, purple felt tip. Across the top card: Week five. House rules. Every unit I ever worked had a binder of them. The good ones were thin.
Write it where the next nurse will find it.
Asha's first card said: The house rules lived at the nurses' station, not in the charge nurse's head. If only one person knows a rule, the unit doesn't have it.

Under it Priya wrote what the GitHub docs say. Repository wide custom instructions go in a Markdown file named copilot-instructions.md in the repository's .github folder. Copilot adds them automatically to requests made in the context of that repository, so nobody has to repeat them in every prompt. You don't see them in the chat, but when Copilot Chat used them, the file is listed in the response's References. They're on by default. Each person can turn them off for their own chat in the editor's settings, and a repository setting controls whether Copilot code review uses them.

Write them as short, self contained statements: what the project is, the languages, frameworks, and versions, how to build and test, and the coding rules. Skip instructions that send Copilot to outside documents, demand a response style, or ask it to "be accurate." There are other levels. Organization owners on Copilot Business or Enterprise can set organization instructions, which work on GitHub.com in Chat, code review, and the cloud agent. Personal instructions apply only to you, and only in Copilot Chat on GitHub.com. Every relevant set is sent. When they conflict, GitHub's docs rank personal first, then repository, then organization, but the safer move is not to write conflicting rules at all. Copilot is non deterministic, so it may not follow every instruction the same way every time. And in VS Code, custom instructions aren't used for inline suggestions as you type.

How the exam asks it. Know the path, .github/copilot-instructions.md, and the three levels: personal, repository, organization. Instructions shape chat, agents, and review. Inline suggestions in VS Code don't use them.
The second card: The ICU's rules aren't the ER's rules. Don't make the ER read the ICU's binder.

Path specific instructions are for rules that only matter in part of a codebase. They go in files whose names end in .instructions.md, in or under .github/instructions. Each one starts with a front matter block that sets applyTo to a glob pattern: infra/**/*.tf for Terraform files anywhere under infra, or **/*.ts,**/*.tsx for every TypeScript file, with commas between patterns. A single star matches files in one folder. Two stars reach every folder below. When the file Copilot is working on matches, it uses the path specific instructions and the repository wide ones together.

Support varies by surface, and the exam likes that. In VS Code and Visual Studio, Copilot Chat uses path specific files. On GitHub.com they're used by the cloud agent and by Copilot code review, but not by Copilot Chat. A file can opt out of one of those two with excludeAgent in its front matter, set to "code-review" or "cloud-agent." Copilot can also read agent instructions from AGENTS.md files, a format several AI agents share, where the nearest one in the folder tree wins. Inside the repository level, GitHub ranks path specific files first, then the repository wide file, then AGENTS.md, and still sends all of them. Support for AGENTS.md differs by feature and editor, so check the current docs before you count on it.

How the exam asks it. If a scenario needs rules for only some files, the answer is a .instructions.md file with applyTo. If the path matches, both the path specific and the repository wide instructions apply.
A protocol can't sign the chart.
The third card: A protocol tells you what to look for. It can't sign the chart for you.

Copilot code review reads your instructions files, which is how a team sets its own review standards. On GitHub.com, it uses the repository wide file and any path specific files that match the changed code. In VS Code and Visual Studio, code review reads only the repository wide file. GitHub's advice for review instructions is plain: short, imperative bullets under clear headings, with a small example of the right and wrong pattern. Start with ten to twenty instructions, test them on real pull requests, and add more a few at a time. Keep any single file to about a thousand lines at most, because in long files some instructions get overlooked.

Some instructions don't work in review at all. Copilot code review won't change the format of its comments, rewrite its overview comment, follow links to outside standards, or change its core function, such as blocking a merge until its comments are resolved. Vague requests like "don't miss any issues" only add noise. Enforcement belongs to branch protection and rulesets, which can also request a Copilot review automatically. One more detail: Copilot reads instructions from the pull request's own branch, not the base branch, so you can test a change to the rules in the same pull request that makes it. It also means a change to an instructions file deserves the same review as any code.
How the exam asks it. Instructions tell Copilot code review what to look for. They don't block merges or follow links. Pick specific checks with examples, and put enforcement in rulesets.
The fourth card: We had order sets for the things we did every night. Same steps for every nurse, so nobody was inventing it at three in the morning.

Prompt files are Copilot's order sets: reusable prompts saved as Markdown files ending in .prompt.md, by default in .github/prompts. Instructions go with every request. A prompt file runs when you call it. In VS Code you type a slash and the prompt's name in chat. An optional front matter block can set a description, the agent or model to use, and which tools it may call. A prompt file can link to other files, including instructions files, with Markdown links or #file. Prompt files are in public preview and work in VS Code, Visual Studio, and JetBrains IDEs, not on GitHub.com. GitHub.com has its own way to share context: a Copilot Space gathers repositories, code, issues, pull requests, notes, and files, so Chat answers from that set, and an organization's space can be shared with its members.

The rest of the card was the chat box itself. Chat participants, typed with bring a specialty: @github for GitHub skills, @terminal for the terminal, @vscode for the editor. Slash commands handle common jobs: /explain, /fix, /tests, /doc in some editors, /clear for a fresh chat, and /help. Watch /new: on GitHub.com it starts a new conversation, but in VS Code it scaffolds a new project. Type a slash to see what your editor offers, because the list varies. Chat variables, typed with add context on purpose: #file, #selection, and in VS Code #codebase for the whole project. Older docs and some exam questions use @workspace for that same idea. And chat has limits: answers can be wrong, history fills the context window, and you can rate a response with a thumbs up or down.
How the exam asks it. Instructions are always on. Prompt files run on demand. Know the three tools in the chat box: participants, slash commands, and context variables.
The last card: Don't describe a good chart to a new nurse. Show them three.

Microsoft Learn sums up good prompts as four S's. Single: one task per prompt. Specific: explicit and detailed. Short: clear without overload. Surround: descriptive file names and the right files open. GitHub's own advice lines up: start general, then add specifics; give examples; break big jobs into small ones; avoid vague words like "this"; point to the relevant code; and iterate. A prompt with no examples is zero shot, which works for common patterns. One example is one shot. Several is few shot, which is best when the format has to be exact. When the real data is sensitive, invent the examples. Learn also names two more. Role prompting tells Copilot to act as a kind of expert, like a security reviewer. Chain prompting builds a feature over several turns, which is exactly when history needs watching.

Then the flow. Copilot builds each prompt from what you typed plus context: the current file, the selected code, open tabs, instructions files, and the chat history. It goes through the proxy and its filters, to the model, and back through filters before you see it. The history rides along with every request, so in a long thread old turns keep steering new answers. Keep history relevant: a new thread for a new task, a short summary of the decisions that still matter, and delete requests that didn't help. Telling Copilot to ignore earlier turns doesn't take them out of what it's sent.
How the exam asks it. Know zero, one, and few shot, the four S's, and why a fresh thread fixes answers that keep drifting back to old turns.

At nine she put the list on the screen in the small conference room. Joyce had coffee. Devin had his laptop closed in front of him, which was new. Ken stood by the door. He had somewhere to be and had come anyway.
These are good. Where do they live, so Copilot actually reads them? I'm not paying for a tool that has to be told the same thing ninety times a day.
And wherever they live, I want to be able to show Nora who changed them, and when.
The team has eleven house rules for Copilot, and Joyce wants them read every time. Where should they live?
Answer. Have each engineer paste them into their own personal instructions.
B. Put them in the .github/copilot-instructions.md file in the Lumen repo.
C. Add them as Copilot organization instructions across every Halcyon repo.
D. Pin them as a message at the top of the engineering channel for everyone.

She creates the Copilot instructions file in Lumen's .github folder on a branch and opens a pull request, so the rules get reviewed like code. Ken likes that the history will show every change and who made it. Joyce asks how they'll know Copilot read it. When Chat uses it, the file shows up in the answer's references.

That's the move. Repository wide custom instructions live in .github/copilot-instructions.md. Copilot adds them to requests made in the context of that repository, and a Chat response that used them lists the file under References. Because it's a file in the repo, it's reviewed and versioned like any other code.
Decision two. Things Lumen Doesn't Tell You.
By Monday afternoon the file existed, and it was empty.

Joyce sent her a link to an old wiki page called Things Lumen Doesn't Tell You. It ran to eleven screens: the history of every product decision, a long section on why the scheduler retries, a joke about a holiday party, and, halfway down, the date rule, in the middle of a paragraph.

I wrote that at two in the morning in 2023, the night of our first clock change bug. I wrote addCalendarDays the same night. She said it lightly, and she didn't look at Priya while she said it. Nobody's opened the page since. I checked.
Can we paste it in? All of it's still true.
Joyce's old wiki page runs eleven screens. What belongs in the instructions file?
Answer. Short rules, plus a line pointing Copilot to the wiki for everything else.
B. One line at the top telling Copilot to take extra care with every date.
C. The whole wiki page pasted in as it is, all eleven screens, word for word.
D. A few short rules pulled from the page, the date rule stated plainly.

It takes an hour to get eleven screens down to one page. Short statements under plain headings: what Lumen does, the languages and frameworks, the commands to build and test, and the rules, one line each. The date rule gets two lines and a small example of what to do and what not to. Joyce reads it twice. That's what I meant to write in 2023.

Good. That's the call. Instructions work best as short, self contained statements: a project overview, the stack and versions, coding standards, and how to build and test. They go with every request in the repository, so they should be broadly useful. In long files, some instructions get overlooked.
Tuesday morning the file was open on her second monitor.

Her draft of copilot instructions dot M D, the file in the dot github folder. It says Lumen does discharge forecasting for hospitals, with TypeScript services, PostgreSQL, and Terraform in the infra folder, and to run npm ci, then npm test, with date tests set to Denver time. Then three rules: a discharge window is calendar days in the hospital's time zone, so use the add calendar days helper and never multiply days by a fixed day length; build SQL with parameters, never by joining strings; and log request IDs, never request bodies.

Anders read it over her shoulder at ten, coffee in hand. Fine. Now where do mine go? Always plan before apply. Never the flag that skips the yes or no question. The staging database has prevent_destroy on it and it stays that way.
He tapped the screen. Not in there, though. Forty people writing TypeScript don't need my state files in every answer they get.
He'd written the first of those rules himself, two weeks ago, under his own name.
Anders's Terraform rules shouldn't reach forty people writing TypeScript. Where should they go?
Answer. Have Anders keep them in his own personal instructions in Chat.
B. Add them to the repository wide instructions file under a Terraform heading.
C. Put them in .github/instructions/terraform.instructions.md with applyTo infra.
D. Leave those rules with Anders, who reviews every infra pull request.

The file is six lines under a short front matter block, with an applyTo line that points it at every Terraform file under infra. Copilot uses it, along with the repository wide file, whenever the file in play matches that pattern, and nowhere else. Anders opens the staging module, asks Copilot Chat what it does, and reads the answer while his coffee goes cold. It knows about prevent_destroy now. That's more than the last contractor knew. He's the last contractor. He lets her laugh at that.

Exactly right. Path specific instructions live in .github/instructions/, in files ending .instructions.md, with an applyTo glob in the front matter, such as infra/**/*.tf. When the file Copilot is working on matches, those instructions are used together with the repository wide ones. Rules for one part of the code stay out of every other request.
Wednesday morning Devin waved her over to his desk.
The yellow page that said Careful was taped to the bottom of his monitor, turned so it faced him and not the room.
The file doesn't work. Watch. In a scratch file he typed const end new Date(start.getTime() and stopped. Gray text appeared after the cursor: days 86400000.
It's right there in the rules. Never multiply by 86400000. And it suggests it anyway.
Copilot's inline suggestion breaks the date rule in the instructions file. What should Priya tell Devin?
Answer. Rewrite the date rule in capital letters at the top of the file.
B. Check his VS Code settings, confirm custom instructions are on and retry.
C. Turn off inline suggestions in the Lumen repo until the file starts working.
D. Explain that inline suggestions skip the file and test the rule in Chat.

She has him ask Copilot Chat to finish the same line. The answer uses addCalendarDays in the hospital's time zone, and under References is Lumen's instructions file. So the gray text never saw it. Not in VS Code. The file shapes chat, agents, and reviews, not suggestions as you type. That part's still yours. Devin deletes the gray text and types the helper name himself.

That's the move. In VS Code, custom instructions aren't used for inline suggestions as you type. They're added to chat requests, agent work, and code review, and when Chat uses them the file, .github/copilot-instructions.md, shows in the response's References. Knowing where instructions apply tells you where review still has to catch things.
Wednesday afternoon Renata and Devin brought her the part of the file meant for Copilot code review. They'd written it together. Priya noticed that, and didn't mention it.
It started from Friday's review rule, the one with whoever wrote it in bold, and tried to teach Copilot the same habits.

Their review section, five lines. Flag day math that multiplies by a fixed day length and suggest the add calendar days helper in the hospital's zone, and flag SQL built by joining strings and suggest a parameterized query. Then block merging until every Copilot comment is resolved, review against the standards at a link to the team wiki, and be thorough and don't miss anything.
Is this how you do it? I wasn't sure which of these it can actually do.
Renata and Devin drafted five lines for Copilot code review. Which should stay, and how?
Answer. Cut the section, delete the five lines and rely on its built in checks.
B. Keep the two specific checks with examples and move blocking into a ruleset.
C. Keep all five lines as written for Copilot code review to enforce.
D. Keep all five lines, each one trimmed short for the review section.

They keep the first two lines and add a short right and wrong code example under each. The wiki line goes, because Copilot code review doesn't follow outside links. "Be thorough" goes, because it doesn't tell Copilot anything. Merge blocking moves where it belongs, to a branch ruleset that requires a human approval and resolved comments. Renata writes the reason for each cut in her notebook, one per line.

Good. That's the call. Copilot code review uses repository instructions and works best with short, specific checks and examples. It doesn't follow external links, change its core behavior such as blocking merges, or get better from vague directives. Enforcement belongs in branch rules and rulesets, which can require approvals and resolved comments.
Thursday at seven Tomasz had his camera on. He had something to show her.
After last week, my team wrote date tests for every service. I read them all. Seven engineers, seven prompts, seven kinds of test. One of them only tested October. Can we have one way to ask?
Behind him his engineers had their editors open, and two of them were already typing.
Seven engineers used seven prompts for date tests, and one only tested October. How should the team standardize?
Answer. Save one shared .prompt.md file in the repo for anyone to run from Chat.
B. Pin the strongest prompt in the Kraków channel for people to copy as needed.
C. Put the full test prompt in the repository wide instructions, always on.
D. Assign the coding agent one issue per service to write all the tests.

Tomasz's best engineer writes date-tests.prompt.md: a one line description in the front matter, then the steps. State the rule first, list the edges, take expected values from the rule, never from current output. It links to the instructions file instead of copying it. In VS Code anyone types a slash and date-tests in chat and gets the same start. Tomasz asks the right question. And on GitHub? Prompt files are for the IDE. VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains. The cloud agent reads the instructions files instead.

Exactly right. Prompt files are reusable prompts saved as .prompt.md files, by default in .github/prompts. You run one in chat when you need that task, so everyone starts from the same prompt. They're in public preview, in VS Code, Visual Studio, and JetBrains IDEs. Instructions apply to every request; a prompt file applies when you call it.

At 10:14 Ken's scanner flagged a pull request. It read every pull request at Halcyon for secrets, patient identifiers, and a list of bad patterns Ken had been adding to for years, and it was rarely wrong. This one was Renata's.

She'd been writing a second prompt file, for test fixtures. Asked once with no examples, Copilot had given her fixtures in the wrong shape: one date field instead of three, times with no zones. So she'd pasted five rows from the staging database into the prompt as examples. Staging was seeded from scrubbed data, mostly. Two of the rows still had real looking dates of birth.
Renata reached Priya's desk a minute before Ken's message did.
I'm closing it. I only wanted it to see the format. Am I in trouble?
Renata's few shot examples came from staging rows with real looking birth dates. How should she fix the prompt?
Answer. Move the rows into a repo file and link to it from the prompt file.
B. Keep the real rows but mask the names and IDs before using them.
C. Drop the examples and describe the format in words, field by field.
D. Swap in three invented rows in the same shape as the real ones.

You're not in trouble. The scanner did its job, and so did you, coming here. They write three fixtures by hand, all invented: an admission at 11:58 PM, one at the first 1:30 on a clock change night, one at noon, each with three date fields and a time zone. Under them, one line: vary the times and zones, keep the shape. Copilot's next twenty fixtures match. Ken approves the new pull request with one word. Better.

That's the move. Few shot prompting gives Copilot several examples of what you want, which works well when the format is exact. Zero shot, with no examples, relies on its training and suits common patterns. When the real data is sensitive, the examples should be made up.
At the Thursday sync Renata put her hand halfway up, then down, then up again.
Priya saw it the first time and stopped talking. Renata.

This is probably basic. I asked Chat what's wrong with this window, and it told me about the export query. Then Devin asked the same question on his laptop and got the right answer. Why would it answer us differently?
Devin turned his laptop around: one file open, the window function selected. Renata had nine tabs open. Three of them were the old export.
Renata and Devin asked Chat the same question and got different answers. What should Renata change?
Answer. Switch Chat to a larger model that can take in a repository this size.
B. Close the unrelated tabs and select the function before asking again.
C. Add #codebase to the question and let it search the whole repo first.
D. Ask the same question several times and go with the most common answer.

Renata closes six tabs, selects calculateWindow, and asks what's wrong with calculateWindow. The answer is about calculateWindow. So 'this' was doing a lot of work. Half the room laughs, kindly, and two people quietly close tabs of their own.

Good. That's the call. Copilot builds its prompt from your question plus context: the open file, the selected code, other open tabs, and the chat history. Open what matters, close what doesn't, select the code, and avoid vague words like "this." Chat variables such as #selection or #file make the context explicit.
Decision nine. One prompt, five jobs.
Friday morning Devin had a chat open with a single prompt in it.

A message from Devin's prompt. Refactor the nightly census job to use parameterized queries the way we fixed the export, add tests for every edge case, update the docs, make it faster, and fix anything else you see.
The answer was six hundred lines across eleven files. Devin scrolled to the bottom and back up.
I can't review this. I mean I can. Not carefully.
Devin's one prompt asks for a refactor, tests, docs, speed and anything else. What should Devin do?
Answer. Run the same prompt again, adding the word carefully to the start.
B. Keep one prompt but spell out what each of the five parts needs.
C. Split it into single task prompts and check each one before the next.
D. Accept all six hundred lines, open the PR and let review catch the rest.

He starts over. First prompt: rewrite the census query with parameters, nothing else. He reads it, runs the tests, commits. Then tests for the census job, naming the edges. Then the docs. By noon it's three small commits instead of one big one, each something a reviewer can actually read. Performance waits for next week, with a ticket.
Exactly right. Good prompts are single, specific, and short, with the right context around them. Break complex work into simple steps and validate each one before building on it.

At one Priya asked Copilot Chat to draft her summary for Joyce: what the house rules were, where they lived, and how they worked. She'd used the same chat thread all week, since seven on Monday morning.
The draft was mostly right. It also described the eleven rules the way she'd first sketched them on Monday, before anyone had read them, three of which the team had cut by Tuesday.
Her own chat history, she realized, had more of Monday in it than Friday.
Priya's Chat draft for Joyce describes rules the team cut by Tuesday. What should she do?
Answer. Start a new chat thread with the final files attached and ask again.
B. Tell it, in the same thread, to ignore everything before Wednesday.
C. Fix the draft by hand and keep the same thread for next week's work.
D. Turn off repository instructions in Chat and ask for the draft again.

The new thread starts with the instructions files, the prompt files, and one line about Joyce's question. The summary comes back with this week's rules and none of Monday's. She doesn't delete the old thread. She just stops carrying it.

That's the move. Copilot Chat sends the conversation history as part of the prompt, so stale turns keep steering answers. Start a new thread for a new task, attach the context that matters, or delete requests that no longer help.
At three she opened the pull request with the house rules in it: the repository wide file, Anders's Terraform file, the review section, and two prompt files. Then she sat looking at the reviewer box.
The runbook was open beside her keyboard. All week she'd been crossing out margins as the rules went into files. Nine were gone, the Terraform ones last.
For years the reviewer on nearly everything she wrote had been Anders. She typed his name.

He came over instead of commenting, which he never did. He looked at the runbook, at his own name with a line through it in her pen, a second longer than he needed to. Before I approve this. How do you know Copilot follows any of it?
Priya's house rules pull request is up, with Anders as reviewer. What should come next?
Answer. Merge it now and check next Friday whether Copilot's reviews improved.
B. Add every rule anyone suggested this week, then merge the pull request.
C. Test the file on this branch with the old 86400000 line planted.
D. Merge it today and trust Copilot to follow each rule in the file.

They push a scratch commit to the same branch: the old line, days 86400000, and a query glued together from strings. Copilot code review reads instructions from the pull request's own branch, so the new rules are live for this review before anything merges. It flags the day math and suggests addCalendarDays. It misses the SQL. Anders rewrites that rule with a short example, they run it again, and it catches both. They drop the scratch commit. He approves at 4:40 with one comment. Read it anyway.

Good. That's the call. Copilot may not follow every instruction every time. Start with a small set of specific instructions, test them on real pull requests, and refine what it misses. Copilot code review reads instructions from the head branch, so you can test changes to them before merging.
The house rules merged on Friday afternoon, tested on a pull request with the old bug planted in it on purpose. Anders's approval was the last thing on the page.
Joyce answered her summary at 6:10 with one line. Can I delete the wiki page now?
Priya thought about it longer than the question needed. Leave it. Somebody wrote it at two in the morning.
Ken's last message of the week came at 6:20. The scanner sees pull requests. It never saw what went to Copilot before one was opened. Monday I want to talk about staging.
On the way out Renata stopped her to ask if she could own the fixtures prompt. Priya said yes before she'd finished asking.
It had been a quieter week than the last one, and she'd needed that. She had written more than she'd decided, and for once that felt like the job.
Sunday was dinner in Aurora. Asha's shoes were already by the door, and the kitchen smelled like her grandmother's dal. There was an argument going.
She never measured. She did it by hand.
She measured. With the steel cup. Her father took it down from the shelf, a small dented cup with the lip worn smooth. This one. Two of these of dal. Half of this of jaggery.
Half? Raj. It was never half.

They'd been having this argument, Priya realized, for as long as she could remember. Nobody had written it down, because their mother had been in the kitchen, and then Raj had, and it had never seemed necessary.
Asha's bag on the counter had index cards in it. It always did. Priya took a blank one, and Asha handed her the purple felt tip without being asked.

She wrote while they cooked. Two steel cups of toor dal. Jaggery: half a cup, says Raj. More, says Asha. Tamarind about the size of a thumb. Mustard seeds until they pop. When the card was full she held it up.
Her father took the felt tip and added one line at the bottom, in the square capitals he'd used on job tickets for thirty one years. ASK ASHA.
Asha looked at it for a moment. Then she took the pen back and wrote underneath, smaller. Ask Raj.
Most of the margins in her runbook had been rules, and rules belonged in a file. A few had been questions only a person could answer. Those, she decided, could stay.
Her father put the card on the refrigerator under a magnet from a hardware store that had closed in 1998, and they ate.
